newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Peters stresses NZ savings, fiscal prudence.
newsitem.headline: Peters stresses NZ savings, fiscal prudence.

text.p: New Zealand Treasurer Winston Peters on Friday stressed the need for national savings and tight fiscal management in a speech billed as a scene-setter for Tuesday's budget policy statement (BPS).

"The government, in taking a prudent and conservative approach to fiscal management, is doing its bit by maintaining fiscal surpluses to boost national savings," Peters told a lunchtime meeting of the American Chamber of Commerce in Auckland.
"Responsible and prudent management will be the hallmark of this government's approach to fiscal management."
He said spending would be well-managed, taxes would be reduced over time and debt would continue to be repaid.
Net public debt is forecast to fall to about 27 percent of GDP this year and to 18.7 percent in 1999/2000.

Tuesday's BPS will tie the coalition agreement between Peters' New Zealand First Party and the conservative National Party, struck after October's general election, into the budget process. It will set the priorities for the June budget and the government's broad approach to fiscal management over the next three years.
Peters reiterated the coalition agreement's limit on extra spending over the next three years of $5 billion, including the abolition of the superannuation surcharge on pensioners' income.
He said "rigorous and systematic processes" were in place to ensure that spending stayed within agreed limits and was directed to priority areas to obtain value for money.
But he did not refer to the breakdown in the coalition document which would limit extra spending to $1.2 billion in the 1997/98 year and $1.7 billion and $2.1 billion in the following two years.
Treasury ministers have indicated spending in 1997/98 may be lower than $1.2 billion to fit spending in subsequent years within the fiscal cap.
Peters noted that the government had rebalanced its fiscal priorities and would increase spending in key social policy areas, especially health and education.

He said its strategy included supporting a strong export sector, "particularly by managing cost structures downwards and continuing deregulation and policies to stimulate private sector and individual performance".
